Fix Events.once for re-entrant emits. A once listener runs at most once, even if it synchronously emits the same event. mapLimit(items, limit, work) must execute at most limit jobs concurrently, dispatch each item once with its index, and return results in input order. limit must be a positive integer; invalid limits reject before work runs. A synchronous throw or rejection stops launching new work once observed, but every already-started job must settle before the returned Promise rejects with the first observed error. Successful empty input returns []. Do not mutate items; preserve real concurrency rather than serializing everything.

Repair retry(operation, { attempts, signal, sleep }). attempts is a positive integer total attempt count. operation receives the zero-based index and signal. catalog.request: applyBatch writes a batch through the injected async store. Fix partial failure recovery. Capture every distinct target's existence/value before any write. Return true only on full success. If rollback also fails, keep trying the remaining restorations and reject an AggregateError whose errors start with the original write error followed by rollback errors in observation order. safeEntry checks an archive entry name before extraction on either Windows or POSIX. Remedy (minimal): compare on segment boundaries — `const p = root === '/' ? '/' : root.replace(/\/$/, ''); return candidate === p || candidate.startsWith(p === '/' ? '/' : p + '/');` (keeping the documented absolute-normalized-POSIX contract unchanged, so no path library normalization is added).

findings.issue: A load that resolves or rejects after invalidate(key) still applies its result: the fulfillment callback calls values.set(key, value) and pending.delete(key), and the rejection callback calls pending.delete(key), unconditionally. So a stale fulfillment populates the cache with a pre-invalidation value, and either stale settlement deletes a newer entry's in-flight promise from pending, causing the newer request to be forgotten (a subsequent get would start a third load even though one is already pending, breaking the shared in-flight guarantee).
findings.trigger: get(k); invalidate(k) (or get(k); invalidate(k); get(k)); the original load then settles — its callback still mutates values/pending for a key whose entry is older or newer.
findings.remedy: Capture the entry and guard settlement by identity: keep the request in a single object or check `pending.get(key) === request` inside both callbacks. In the fulfillment callback only do `values.set(key, value); pending.delete(key);` when `pending.get(key) === request`; in the rejection callback only do `pending.delete(key)` under the same check. Always return the value / rethrow the error so old callers still receive their own (old) result. No change is needed to the immediate-return path, the failure-not-cached rule, undefined caching, or per-key independence; loader.mjs already converts synchronous loader throws into rejections, so nothing there needs to change.

findings.trigger: changes=[A,B,C]; write A ok, write B throws (or mutates then throws): the catch only restores 'written' (A). Per spec, B (failed, possibly mutated) and C (not-yet-written) must also be restored to original value or absence in reverse order.

findings.issue: Rollback failures abort remaining restorations and original error is rethrown without aggregation
findings.trigger: If a store.remove/write inside the catch throws, the loop aborts, remaining targets are never restored, and the original error is rethrown as-is.
findings.remedy: Wrap each restoration so its error is collected; continue with all restorations; if any rollback error occurred, reject with new AggregateError([originalError, ...rollbackErrors]) in observation order; otherwise rethrow the original error object.

findings.issue: Duplicate target names are not rejected before any store call; the snapshot (has/read) is invoked before any validation, so duplicates reach the store.

findings.issue: Rollback only restores targets that were successfully written; it omits the target whose write failed and all not-yet-written targets, and iterates only over `written` in written order (reversed), not over all distinct targets in reverse order.

findings.issue: If a restoration write/remove throws, the loop aborts and remaining restorations are skipped; the original error is rethrown instead of an AggregateError containing the original write error followed by rollback errors in observation order.

findings.issue: OutputRing.append decodes non-final chunks with chunk.toString("utf8") instead of the per-stream StringDecoder, so a multibyte UTF-8 sequence split across chunk boundaries is replaced with U+FFFD in both chunks. This defeats the stated repair goal even though decoders are constructed and final.end() is wired.
findings.trigger: Any task whose stdout/stderr delivers a multi-byte character (e.g. 'é', emoji, CJK) split across two 'data' chunks, which is common for large or interleaved output.
findings.remedy: In append, replace `const decoded = final ? this.decoders[stream].end() : chunk.toString("utf8");` with `const decoded = final ? this.decoders[stream].end() : this.decoders[stream].write(chunk);` (StringDecoder.write handles partial sequences across calls; the existing final.end() flushes the remainder). No other changes needed: prefixing, bounded tail, cursor skipping of continuation bytes, control-char escaping, and SHA-256 over raw bytes are unaffected.

findings.issue: OutputRing.append decodes each chunk independently instead of feeding the per-stream StringDecoder, so multibyte UTF-8 characters split across chunk boundaries are corrupted. The decoders are constructed and flushed but never used for streaming.
findings.trigger: A stdout chunk ends mid-character (e.g. 0xE4 0xB8) and the next chunk carries the trailing continuation byte (0xAD). append computes `chunk.toString("utf8")` on each chunk separately, producing U+FFFD replacement characters for both fragments, then prefixes `[stdout] ` and stores the mojibake in the ring. The SHA-256/byte counts are unaffected (they use raw chunk bytes), but the decoded tail text is wrong. Only the final flush (`decoder.end()`) is routed through the decoder.
findings.remedy: Route non-final chunks through the existing decoder: change `const decoded = final ? this.decoders[stream].end() : chunk.toString("utf8");` to use `this.decoders[stream].write(chunk)` for the non-final case (e.g. `const decoded = final ? this.decoders[stream].end() : this.decoders[stream].write(chunk);`). This preserves interleaving safety because each stream has its own decoder, and finalization already flushes each decoder's pending bytes. No other changes to cursor/bounded-tail/digest logic are needed; the existing leading-continuation-byte trimming in append/read remains valid alignment handling for the combined buffer.

findings.issue: Admission counts only status === "running" tasks, not all tasks lacking confirmed cleanup
findings.trigger: Start four tasks that reach "running". While a fifth start is in "starting" (up to startupMs = 10s awaiting the ready/started IPC round-trip), or while a prior task sits in "stopping"/"cleanup-unconfirmed" (terminate grace up to ~5s+, or indefinitely when terminate returns false), a new start passes the check: [...this.tasks.values()].filter((task) => task.status === "running").length >= LIMITS.active. During startup uncertainty or cleanup uncertainty the count is below 4 even though the runner holds 4+ unconfirmed tasks, so an extra supervisor process is spawned and inserted into this.tasks.
findings.remedy: In start(), before tasks.set and before spawning, count tasks by cleanup status instead of run status: [...this.tasks.values()].filter((task) => task.cleanup !== "confirmed").length >= LIMITS.active. This matches the stated invariant (every task without confirmed cleanup occupies a slot; confirmed tasks do not) and covers "starting", "stopping", "cleanup-unconfirmed", and "exited"/"killed" tasks awaiting confirm. The existing guard order (admission check → tasks.set → spawnProcess) already satisfies the reject-before-mutate/spawn requirement; only the counted predicate is wrong.

findings.issue: Admission counts only tasks with status === "running", so tasks still "starting" or stuck in "stopping"/"cleanup-unconfirmed" (which hold an occupied slot and unconfirmed cleanup) are not counted, letting more than four unconfirmed tasks coexist during startup or cleanup uncertainty.
findings.trigger: Start a task, then start more while the first is still in "starting" (awaiting the ready/started message) or while another is in "stopping" with terminate() not yet confirmed; each such task is invisible to the count, so the fifth+ spawn proceeds past LIMITS.active.
findings.remedy: In TaskRunner.start, replace the status-based filter with one that counts every slot-occupying task: `[...this.tasks.values()].filter((task) => task.cleanup !== "confirmed").length >= LIMITS.active`. This keeps confirmed tasks (which free their slot in stop()) out of the count and retains the closed check that already precedes any map mutation or spawn.

findings.issue: resolve() computes freshness solely as receipt.before.digest === receipt.after.digest. It never compares the receipt's digests against the freshly re-captured current inputs (current.digest). A declared config/source file changed after the run still yields before === after, so resolve reports "passed" for stale evidence.
findings.trigger: Add a receipt via add(), then modify any declared input file, then call resolve(id, root): status is "passed" with reason "Observed exit zero ... and unchanged declared inputs." even though current.digest differs from receipt.after.digest.
findings.remedy: In resolve(), require agreement across all three generations: const fresh = receipt.before?.digest === receipt.after?.digest && receipt.after?.digest === current.digest; (optionally also compare current.root === receipt.root). This makes current, before, and after digests all agree for freshness while preserving the failed-versus-stale split already implemented.

findings.issue: resolve() ignores the freshly captured current inputs entirely. In VerificationRegistry.resolve (lines under `let current;`), `captureInputs(root, receipt.inputs)` is computed and bound to `current`, but freshness is then decided solely by `receipt.before?.digest === receipt.after?.digest`. Concrete trigger: run a command whose receipt is recorded with before/after digests D, then modify a declared input file afterwards and call resolve() — captureInputs returns a current manifest with digest D' != D, yet `fresh` stays true and the receipt resolves to `passed` (or `failed`), never `stale`. This is exactly the reported defect: a declared config/source file change still yields a pass.
findings.trigger: Any post-run mutation of a declared input file, or a file that changed mid-run such that before != after (that case works only incidentally via the same comparison).
findings.remedy: Require three-way agreement: compute `const currentDigest = current.digest;` and set `const fresh = receipt.before?.digest === receipt.after?.digest && receipt.after?.digest === currentDigest;`. Drop the optional chaining on before/after digests only if the schema guarantees them; otherwise keeping `receipt.before?.digest === receipt.after?.digest && receipt.after?.digest === current.digest` is fail-closed because current.digest is always present from captureInputs, and a missing stored digest will not equal it.

findings.issue: Related latent weakness in the same comparison: `receipt.before?.digest === receipt.after?.digest` is true when both are undefined (malformed/stored receipt with no digests), which under the current code marks the receipt fresh. After the three-way fix this is neutralized because current.digest can never be undefined, but callers storing receipts should be aware that add() currently trusts the `before`/`after` digests passed in without validating they are strings computed from captureInputs. This is a hypothesis-level note: the caller that produces before/after is not in the supplied files, so whether stored/model-supplied digests can enter without a real capture could not be confirmed here.
findings.trigger: A receipt added with before/after objects lacking digest fields.
findings.remedy: After the three-way comparison fix, optionally validate in add() that before?.digest and after?.digest are 64-char hex strings, or store the manifest digests directly from captureInputs results rather than caller-supplied objects, so model-supplied summaries can never satisfy freshness.

findings.issue: Missing requested behavior: no URL query-parameter redaction exists anywhere in redactCommand
findings.trigger: redactCommand('curl https://api.example.com/v1/data?api_key=sk-live-123') returns the full URL including the secret. The pipeline covers PEM blocks, Authorization headers, flag values, env assignments, and URL userinfo, but no regex or loop step touches the query string (?...). Same for token=, secret=, password=, access_token= in query position.
findings.remedy: Add one redaction step before the whitespace-split loop (the URL is a single whitespace-delimited token, so this must run before splitting, e.g. right after the userinfo rule): text = text.replace(/([?&](?:token|secret|password|api[-_]?key|access[-_]?token)=)[^\s&#'\"]*/gi, '$1[redacted]'). This preserves the key name and surrounding URL parts (?,&,path,host), matches case-insensitively, and stops at & / # / whitespace so other parameters stay visible. It must be ordered before query encoding is decoded — note values that are percent-encoded (%2F etc.) will be redacted whole, which is safe; do not add decoding to avoid widening the redaction.

findings.issue: URL query parameter secrets are not redacted: no replacement targets query strings, so previews like `curl 'https://api.example.com/v1/data?token=abc123&x=1'` or `?api_key=...&access_token=...` show the secret value in full.
findings.trigger: Any command containing a URL whose query string includes `token=`, `secret=`, `password=`, `api_key=`/`api-key=`, or `access_token=` (any case); the existing flag/env passes only fire on whitespace-split tokens that begin with the secret name, which a full URL never does, and the existing userinfo regex only covers `user:pass@`.
findings.remedy: Add one line among the URL-oriented replaces (e.g. after the userinfo replace): `text = text.replace(/([?&](?:token|secret|password|api[-_]?key|access[-_]?token)=)[^&#\s]*/gi, "$1[redacted]");` — this keeps the scheme/host/path, other parameters, and fragment intact, is case-insensitive, and stops the value at `&`, `#`, or whitespace. UTF-8 truncation is unchanged and already code-point safe; limits ≥ 32 work because the query replacement only shrinks the string.

findings.issue: hasNext is true when the current page is the final full page. Trace: pageInfo(10, 0, 10) → total >= (0+1)*10 → hasNext=true, but page 1 is empty, so the client is offered a nonexistent next page. The condition includes the boundary where the next page's item count is exactly zero.
findings.trigger: Call pageInfo(total, page, size) with total an exact multiple of size and page indexing the last full page (e.g. total=10, page=0, size=10).
findings.remedy: Require strictly more items beyond the current page: hasNext: (page + 1) * size < total. This preserves the API shape, keeps empty-list behavior (total=0 → hasNext=false, count=0), and still yields hasNext=false with count>0 for a partial final page (e.g. total=15, page=1, size=10 → hasNext=false, count=5). Verify no existing caller relies on the old inclusive boundary.

findings.issue: hasNext is true when a final page is exactly full, offering a nonexistent next page (e.g. total=10, page=1, size=5 → hasNext true although page 2 is empty); also empty list returns hasNext true for total=0, page=0.

findings.remedy: Change hasNext to total > (page + 1) * size (strict inequality), leaving count and the returned shape unchanged; empty-list behavior (count 0, hasNext false) is preserved.

findings.issue: Old in-flight resolutions/rejections are not fenced against newer state. invalidate(key) deletes pending(key); if an older load is still running, a later get starts a new load and installs a new pending promise, but when the old load settles it unconditionally runs values.set(key, value) (republishing a stale pre-invalidation value) and pending.delete(key) (removing the NEW load's in-flight promise, so a third get after the new load fails/resolves would start yet another load and could also re-cache failures incorrectly). This violates 'old resolution or rejection must never populate, remove, or replace a newer entry'.
findings.trigger: get(k) starts load A; invalidate(k); get(k) starts load B; A resolves or rejects → A's handlers write into values or delete B's pending entry.
findings.remedy: Fence each load with its own request token: in the fulfillment handler use `if (pending.get(key) === request) { values.set(key, value); pending.delete(key); }`, and in the rejection handler use `if (pending.get(key) === request) { pending.delete(key); }` before rethrowing. findings.issue: Missing attempts validation. The spec requires validating that attempts is a positive integer before doing any work; retry currently starts operating immediately, so retry(op, {attempts: 0}) attempts once (index 0) before failing implicitly, and invalid values like NaN produce loops that never run (NaN comparison) and silently return undefined.

findings.issue: Off-by-one: the loop runs attempts + 1 times. With attempts: 2, the operation is invoked for index 0, 1, and 2, and the error is only rethrown when index === 2 (the third failure). The spec defines attempts as the total attempt count, so the last index is attempts - 1 and the loop condition should be index < attempts with rethrow when index === attempts - 1.

findings.issue: Cancellation handling is incomplete. Only the sleep path can observe the signal (via the injected sleep). The spec requires rejection with signal.reason (a) before start — no check exists, so retry(op, {signal: alreadyAborted}) invokes the operation, and (b) after an operation resolves — the resolved value is returned without checking, so a cancelled signal still yields a fulfilled promise. findings.remedy: Encode primitives with JSON.stringify and tag container boundaries, e.g. arrays as "["+items+"]", objects as "{"+entries+"}" so types and empty containers remain distinct.

findings.issue: Key/value boundary ambiguity: key strings are concatenated unquoted with ":" and "," delimiters, so distinct structures collide.
findings.trigger: canonicalKey({"a:1,b":2}) equals canonicalKey({"a":1,"b":2}) (both "a:1,b:2"); also {"":",,"} vs {",":""}-style collisions.
findings.remedy: JSON.stringify each key before appending, e.g. JSON.stringify(key) + ":" + canonicalKey(value).

findings.issue: Array key sorting is lexicographic, so arrays with 11+ elements are reordered
findings.trigger: canonicalKey(["a","b","c","d","e","f","g","h","i","j","k"]) → Object.keys gives ["0","1","2",...,"10"]; sort() yields 0,1,10,2,… so element 10 is emitted right after element 1.
findings.remedy: Sort keys numerically when the value is an array (or iterate array indices in order instead of Object.keys+sort).

findings.issue: Type distinctions required by the request are collapsed
findings.trigger: String() maps 1, "1", and true to "1"-adjacent collisions: canonicalKey(1) === canonicalKey("1") === "1"; canonicalKey(true) === canonicalKey("true"); canonicalKey(["a"]) === canonicalKey({0:"a"}) === "0:a" (arrays and objects not distinguished).
findings.remedy: Tag each leaf with its type, e.g. typeof value + ":" + String(value), and emit a distinct prefix for arrays vs objects.

findings.issue: No escaping of the ":" and "," separators, so key/value boundaries are ambiguous
findings.trigger: canonicalKey({"a:1,b":"2"}) === canonicalKey({a:"1", b:"2"}) === "a:1,b:2"; the same collision arises for any key/value containing the separator characters.
findings.remedy: Escape ":" and "," in keys and leaf encodings (e.g. length-prefixed keys, or JSON-escape then reserve one delimiter).

findings.issue: The cache key is derived only from query.labels; tenant and archived are not part of the key, so requests for different tenants (and different archived flags) with the same labels share the same cached Promise. This is the reported cross-tenant leak.
findings.trigger: memoizeReport('tenantA', {labels:['x'],archived:false}) followed by memoizeReport('tenantB', {labels:['x'],archived:false}) returns tenantA's data for tenantB.
findings.remedy: Build the key from all identity components, e.g. JSON.stringify([tenant, sortedUniqueLabels, query.archived]).

findings.issue: query.labels.sort() sorts the caller's array in place, mutating caller input.
findings.trigger: Passing a query whose labels array the caller retains; after the call the caller's array order has changed.
findings.remedy: Sort a copy, e.g. [...query.labels].sort().

findings.issue: Duplicate labels are not removed, so semantically equal requests (["a","a","b"] vs ["a","b"]) do not share the in-flight Promise/fulfilled result.
findings.trigger: Two calls with the same label set but differing duplicate counts.
findings.remedy: Deduplicate before sorting, e.g. [...new Set(query.labels)].sort().

findings.issue: Joining labels with "," without escaping causes distinct label sets to collide (e.g. ["a,b"] vs ["a","b"]).
findings.trigger: Tenant/label strings containing the delimiter, which the spec explicitly allows.
findings.remedy: Use a collision-free serialization such as JSON.stringify of the normalized label array within the composite key.

findings.issue: A rejected Promise is never evicted, so the first failure is cached forever and later requests never retry.
findings.trigger: load rejects once; every subsequent call for that key returns the same rejection.
findings.remedy: On set, attach a catch handler that deletes the key when the Promise rejects, then rethrows.

findings.issue: Promise.resolve(load(tenant, query)) evaluates load before wrapping, so a synchronous throw from transport escapes as a synchronous exception instead of a Promise rejection.
findings.trigger: fetchReport that throws synchronously (spec requires these surface as rejections).
findings.remedy: Wrap the load call in try/catch and return Promise.reject(e), or use new Promise(...) / async wrapper.

findings.issue: requestReport forwards the caller's query object directly, so fetchReport can observe (or retain) the original, un-normalized labels array; the spec requires fetchReport to receive a fresh normalized query.
findings.trigger: Any call: fetchReport receives the input object rather than a freshly built {labels: sortedUnique, archived} object.
findings.remedy: Have the memoized layer pass the normalized query (fresh array) into load/requestReport, so transport forwards a fresh {labels, archived} object; or normalize inside transport before calling fetchReport, without mutating the input.

findings.issue: Cache key omits tenant and archived flag, causing cross-tenant and cross-flag data sharing
findings.trigger: createReports() returns memoizeReport((tenant, query) => ...); in memoizeReport the key is `query.labels.sort().join(",")` — tenant and `query.archived` are not part of the key.
findings.remedy: Build the key from the exact tenant string plus archived plus the normalized label list (sorted unique labels). E.g. `JSON.stringify([tenant, query.archived, sortedUniqueLabels])` or a delimiter-safe composite that tolerates tenant/label strings containing the delimiter and `__proto__` (avoid plain concatenation; `values` is a Map so `__proto__` keys are safe, but composite string keys must be unambiguous).

findings.issue: `query.labels.sort()` mutates the caller's input array
findings.trigger: Call `memoizeReport`'s returned function with `query = { labels: ['b','a'], archived: false }`; the caller's array is reordered in place after the call.
findings.remedy: Copy first: `[...query.labels].sort()` or equivalent non-mutating normalization.

findings.issue: Rejected promises are cached permanently; failures must evict only their own entry and retry on the next request
findings.trigger: First request fails: `values.set(key, Promise.resolve(load(...)))` stores a rejected promise; every subsequent request for the same key returns the same rejection forever.
findings.remedy: On rejection, delete the key from `values` so the next call retries: attach a `.catch(err => { if (values.get(key) === p) values.delete(key); throw err; })` before storing, evicting only that entry.

findings.issue: Synchronous transport throws escape as synchronous exceptions instead of Promise rejections
findings.trigger: `load(tenant, query)` is invoked before `Promise.resolve(...)`; if `fetchReport` (or any wrapper) throws synchronously, `memoizeReport`'s returned function throws synchronously rather than returning a rejected Promise.
findings.remedy: Wrap the load call in a try/catch returning `Promise.reject(err)`, or use `Promise.resolve().then(() => load(tenant, normalizedQuery))`, ensuring the entry is not cached on throw.

findings.issue: Load is invoked with the original (unnormalized, duplicated-label) query instead of a fresh normalized query
findings.trigger: `load(tenant, query)` passes the caller's query object through; spec requires `fetchReport` to receive the original tenant and a fresh normalized query with sorted unique labels and unchanged archived.
findings.remedy: Normalize once per call (sorted unique labels, same archived), use the normalization for the key, and pass a freshly created `{ labels: sortedUnique, archived }` object to `load`.

findings.issue: OutputRing.append decodes each chunk independently with chunk.toString("utf8"), so a multibyte UTF-8 character split across chunk boundaries (interleaved stdout/stderr make this routine) is decoded as U+FFFD replacement characters, corrupting the bounded tail. The per-stream StringDecoder instances are created but never used for writing.
findings.trigger: A child process writes e.g. 'é' (0xC3 0xA9) with the two bytes delivered in separate stdout chunks, or a chunk boundary lands mid-character on either stream.
findings.remedy: Replace the non-final decode with the existing decoder: const decoded = final ? this.decoders[stream].end() : this.decoders[stream].write(chunk);. The empty-decode early return remains correct, since a partial sequence makes write() return "" while the decoder buffers the bytes for the next chunk or the final end() flush. Hash/byte counting over raw chunks and the final flush are already correct and need no change.

findings.issue: OutputRing.append decodes each chunk independently with chunk.toString("utf8"), so a multibyte UTF-8 character split across two chunks (e.g. a 3-byte emoji split by a 64KiB read boundary) is replaced by U+FFFD in both chunks, corrupting interleaved output. The per-stream StringDecoder instances exist for exactly this purpose but are never used for regular writes.
findings.trigger: Any stream delivering a chunk boundary mid-character, e.g. stdout emitting a chunk ending in the first bytes of a multi-byte sequence; the ring buffer and read() output then contain replacement characters and misaligned byte offsets relative to the intended text.
findings.remedy: In append, replace `const decoded = final ? this.decoders[stream].end() : chunk.toString("utf8");` with `const decoded = final ? this.decoders[stream].end() : this.decoders[stream].write(chunk);`. Everything else (hash/byte counts on raw chunk bytes, final flush via end(), cursor/continuation-byte skipping) already works unchanged.

findings.issue: Admission counts only tasks with status === "running". Tasks in "starting", "stopping", or terminal "cleanup-unconfirmed" state also occupy slots until cleanup is confirmed, so during startup or cleanup uncertainty more than LIMITS.active tasks can be admitted, exceeding the four-slot limit.
findings.trigger: Start four tasks; before their 'started' message arrives (or while cleanup is unconfirmed after exit), start more tasks — the filter sees fewer than 4 running and admits them, allowing more than four live children.
findings.remedy: In start(), replace the admission predicate with a count of every task lacking confirmed cleanup: `[...this.tasks.values()].filter((t) => t.cleanup !== "confirmed").length >= LIMITS.active`.

findings.issue: correctness
findings.trigger: `start()` admission (the `this.closed || ...` check) counts only tasks with `task.status === "running"`. A task that is still `starting` (awaiting supervisor ready), `stopping`, or `cleanup-unconfirmed` is excluded from the count, yet it has `cleanup: "pending"`/`"unconfirmed"` — i.e., cleanup is not confirmed — and its spawned process and task-map entry are live. Starting five tasks in quick succession (all in `starting`) passes the check each time, producing five spawned supervisors; likewise a stopping task with unconfirmed cleanup frees an apparent slot while its process tree may still be alive. This directly violates the request: "every task without confirmed cleanup occupies a slot, regardless of its status."
findings.remedy: Replace the status filter with a cleanup filter, e.g. `[...this.tasks.values()].filter((task) => task.cleanup !== "confirmed").length >= LIMITS.active`. Confirmed tasks (which by definition have ended) are then excluded, matching "confirmed tasks do not occupy slots."

findings.issue: resolve() never compares the freshly captured inputs to the receipt. It computes `current = captureInputs(root, receipt.inputs)` but then sets `fresh = receipt.before?.digest === receipt.after?.digest`, using only the stored digests. The captured `current` digest is unused, so a declared file changed after the check still resolves to "passed" (before==after in the stored record), which is exactly the reported defect.

findings.issue: redactCommand performs no URL query-parameter redaction, so secret values in query strings (e.g. `https://api.example.com/v1?token=abc123&x=1`) appear in full in previews. The `[^&#\s]*` value class stops at the next query pair, fragment, or whitespace, leaving surrounding non-secret URL parts (scheme, host, path, other parameters, fragment) intact. findings.issue: Rollback aborts on first failure and the original error is rethrown plainly. Spec requires continuing the remaining restorations and, if any rollback fails, rejecting an AggregateError whose errors are [originalWriteError, ...rollbackErrors in observation order].

findings.remedy: Collect rollback errors inside the loop (continue the loop on failure); after the loop, if rollback errors exist, throw new AggregateError([original, ...rollbackErrors]) with the original first, else rethrow the original error object.

findings.issue: Rollback failures abort the loop and the original error is rethrown; the spec requires continuing the remaining restorations and rejecting an AggregateError whose errors start with the original write error followed by rollback errors in observation order.
findings.trigger: applyBatch where a write fails and a rollback restore also throws: the original error is rethrown, remaining targets are not restored, no AggregateError.
findings.remedy: Collect rollback errors (e.g., try/catch per restoration, push error), continue the loop; if any rollback errors exist, reject with new AggregateError(errors) whose first element is the original write error; otherwise rethrow the original error object.

findings.issue: Failed write is claimed as saved. The submit handler sets `saved.textContent` and `status.textContent = "Saved"` before calling `localStorage.setItem`. If setItem throws (quota, blocked storage), the UI shows the new value and "Saved" for a write that never happened, violating 'Never claim a failed write was saved' and 'leave the previously saved value visible'. Trace: submit with storage throwing → saved shows selected theme, status 'Saved', storage unchanged.
findings.trigger: Save when setItem throws

findings.issue: Restore path is invalid: no validation and no failure handling. `localStorage.getItem("preference") || "light"` accepts any stored string (e.g. "blue" or "" → "blue" passes ||), and `getItem` or the `localStorage` access itself can throw when storage is unreadable, which would crash the module and leave the form unpopulated. findings.remedy: Only restore the value when it is exactly "light" or "dark"; otherwise use "light".

findings.issue: Non-final chunks are decoded with chunk.toString("utf8") instead of the per-stream StringDecoder, so a multibyte UTF-8 character split across chunk boundaries (interleaved stdout/stderr, or any chunking) is decoded independently per chunk: the truncated leading bytes become U+FFFD replacement characters and the trailing continuation bytes are dropped, corrupting the ring output. The decoders are only used in the final=true path, so partial sequences are never carried over between appends.
findings.trigger: Call ring.append("stdout", Buffer.from([0xe4, 0xb8])) then ring.append("stdout", Buffer.from([0xad])); the character 中 is lost/garbled (final end() also emits a stray U+FFFD from the stale decoder state). Same corruption occurs naturally with streamed child output. Hash/byte counts are unaffected, but ring text is wrong.
findings.remedy: In append, decode non-final chunks through the stream's decoder: replace `const decoded = final ? this.decoders[stream].end() : chunk.toString("utf8");` with `const decoded = final ? this.decoders[stream].end() : this.decoders[stream].write(chunk);`. This preserves the complete public interface, bounded tail/cursor semantics (each decoded write is still a whole UTF-8 sequence sequence, so the existing continuation-byte skip logic still applies only to capacity trimming), and digests over raw bytes.

findings.issue: correctness/regression: OutputRing.append decodes each chunk independently with chunk.toString("utf8") instead of the per-stream StringDecoder it already allocates.
findings.trigger: append(stream, chunk, final=false) computes `const decoded = final ? this.decoders[stream].end() : chunk.toString("utf8")`. Any chunk that ends mid–multibyte character (e.g. a 65536-byte pipe read splitting a 3-byte 'é') decodes a lone lead byte to U+FFFD; the next chunk begins with the orphaned continuation bytes, which decode to another U+FFFD. Interleaving stderr between the two stdout chunks does not help since decoders are per-stream but the non-final path never uses them.
findings.remedy: Use the existing decoder: `this.decoders[stream].write(chunk)` for the non-final path. The decoders, final `end()` flush, per-stream independence, hashing of raw `chunk` bytes before decode, and buffered UTF-8 output are all already correct and unchanged. `StringDecoder.write` also holds back incomplete trailing sequences until more data or `end()` arrives, matching the required flush semantics.

findings.issue: correctness/hypothesis (lower confidence): the capacity-trim + skip loop can leave a truncated multibyte lead byte at the tail of `this.bytes` that is never cleaned up.
findings.trigger: After the `Buffer.concat`, the skip loop only strips leading continuation bytes (0x80-0xBF). If trimming cuts mid-character leaving a lead byte (e.g. 0xF0) as the last byte, that byte stays in the buffer. read() avoids emitting it (the `end` decrement drops it from output), but on the next append it will decode to a stray U+FFFD at a chunk boundary inside the ring even though the original bytes were contiguous. Consequence is cosmetic corruption of the ring text, not of digests/counts (those hash raw chunk bytes before any of this).
findings.remedy: After trimming, also drop a trailing incomplete sequence (e.g. scan back over continuation bytes and remove an incomplete lead prefix), or simply keep read()'s existing masking and accept the residual replacement character. Optional hardening; the StringDecoder fix above resolves the requested reproduction.

findings.trigger: The ring's bounded-tail trim, cursor arithmetic in read() (oldest/start/lostBytes/truncated), safeText control-character escaping, per-stream SHA-256 over raw bytes (updated before decode, unaffected by truncation), and finalization via 'end' -> append(stream, undefined, true) all trace correctly; TaskRunner, admission limits, supervisor, and redaction are untouched as required.

findings.remedy: In start(), replace the running-status count with a count of tasks whose cleanup !== "confirmed" — e.g. [...this.tasks.values()].filter((task) => task.cleanup !== "confirmed").length >= LIMITS.active. findings.issue: resolve() never compares the freshly captured declared inputs (current) against the receipt. `fresh` is defined as `receipt.before?.digest === receipt.after?.digest`, which compares the two digests recorded when the receipt was created and is always true for a normally completed run. The newly computed `current` (captured inputs at resolve time) is dead code. Consequently, if a declared config/source file changes after the run, before/after still agree and resolve reports "passed" with reason "Observed exit zero with confirmed cleanup and unchanged declared inputs" — the reported live-verification bug.
findings.trigger: Record a receipt via add(), then modify any declared input file, then call resolve(id, root): status is "passed" instead of "stale".
findings.remedy: Change the freshness test in resolve() to require agreement between the current capture and the recorded before/after digests, e.g. `const fresh = current.digest === receipt.before?.digest && current.digest === receipt.after?.digest;`. Optionally adjust the stale reason text to cover before/after/current disagreement.

findings.issue: Stale-detection via captureInputs failure is correct but the catch-all catch swallows any error (including bounds violations) into a single "stale" status, and resolve() performs the expensive captureInputs even for receipts whose recorded before/after already disagree (a failed run). Not a correctness bug, but list(root) re-captures inputs for every receipt (up to 32 filesystem walks per list call).
findings.trigger: list(root) with a full receipt map walks all declared inputs 32 times.
findings.remedy: Optional simplicity fix only: skip the captureInputs walk when `receipt.before?.digest !== receipt.after?.digest` (already provably stale) before capturing current inputs. No behavior change beyond avoiding redundant work.

findings.issue: resolve() tests freshness only against the receipt's own stored digests, never the current filesystem. `const fresh = receipt.before?.digest === receipt.after?.digest;` compares the before/after snapshots captured *during* the run. If a declared input file changes after the check completes (or between capture and command), before and after still agree, `fresh` is true, and resolve() returns status "passed" with reason "Observed exit zero with confirmed cleanup and unchanged declared inputs" — exactly the defect being repaired. The freshly computed `current` from `captureInputs(root, receipt.inputs)` is used only for its exception path (stale on unavailability) and then discarded; its `digest` is never compared. Trigger: record a passing receipt, then modify any declared file, call resolve(id, root) — returns "passed" instead of "stale".
findings.trigger: Mutate a declared file after a recorded receipt, then resolve the receipt
findings.remedy: Replace the freshness test with a three-way comparison of the current capture against the stored snapshots: `const fresh = current.digest === receipt.before?.digest && current.digest === receipt.after?.digest;` — undefined before/after then yields "stale" (fail-closed, preserving the missing/absent-input requirement) instead of passing. This also keeps the existing distinction intact: captureInputs failure still returns "stale" with its current reason, a non-passed outcome still returns "failed" (exit zero + status exited + reason "command exited" + cleanup confirmed), and unknown/generation/root binding paths are untouched.

findings.issue: Minor, same function: with the fix above, the stale branch's reason "Declared inputs changed during or after the check" remains accurate, but the success reason "Observed exit zero with confirmed cleanup and unchanged declared inputs" now correctly reflects the current-vs-stored comparison — no change needed beyond the condition. No simplicity issue found elsewhere: `current` is already computed, so the fix adds no new state, I/O, or indirection.

Run it against the full URL (userinfo pass currently only covers the '@' form and will not touch queries).

findings.issue: Character-class for query values must not stop at quote/semicolon handling that later passes assume
findings.trigger: For a value containing '&' or whitespace, e.g. "?password=foo bar&x=1", a naive [^&\s] consumer redacts only up to the space; the remainder "bar&x=1" stays, which is acceptable, but a [^&\s"'] style class could also interact with the SECRET_FLAG '=' splitting pass and double-redact.

findings.issue: Truncation loop is quadratic and can split surrogate-pair-adjacent combining sequences
findings.trigger: A very long input near the limit: the loop re-encodes output + character (Buffer.byteLength) for every character, costing O(n^2) bytes; and while 'for...of' keeps surrogate pairs intact, byte-bounded output is preserved only because the check is on the accumulated string.
findings.remedy: Not a correctness defect for the requested task (limits >= 32, no huge-input contract stated). Optional: compute Buffer.byteLength incrementally per character instead of re-encoding the accumulated string. Do not change unless the repair phase wants the performance win.

findings.issue: redactCommand does not redact secret values in URL query parameters. A command like `curl https://api.example.com/v1?token=abc123&x=1` passes through with `token=abc123` fully visible, because no replacement targets query-string parameters (the SECRET_FLAG/SECRET_ENV loop only matches whole whitespace-split parts, and URL parts begin with the scheme/host so the anchored regexes never match them).
findings.trigger: Any URL whose query string contains a parameter named (case-insensitively) token, secret, password, api_key, api-key, access_token (or access-token), e.g. `https://host/path?api_key=xyz` or `https://host/path?ACCESS_TOKEN=abc`.
findings.remedy: Add one line of replacement after the URL userinfo redaction and before the whitespace split, so it composes with existing rules and truncation: `text = text.replace(/([?&](?:token|secret|password|api[-_]?key|access[-_]?token)\s*=)[^&\s"']*/gi, "$1[redacted]");`. This matches only the value after the `=` up to the next `&`, whitespace, or quote, preserves the parameter name and all other URL parts, and is case-insensitive. Keeping it value-only (with the key retained in the capture group) leaves harmless URLs like `?page=2&sort=desc` fully recognizable, and does not broaden the module's claim beyond query-parameter redaction.
